subject: portrait photos
title: People Explained Exactly Why They Chose a Face They Had Rejected

scenes.text: People will defend a choice they never made.
In 2005, Swedish researchers showed 120 volunteers pairs of portraits and asked which face was more attractive.
They handed over the chosen photo and asked why. But with a card trick, they sometimes swapped in the rejected face.
About three times out of four, nobody noticed.
They just explained their choice, as confidently and in as much detail as a real one.
It's called choice blindness. You don't always know why you chose something. You only know how to explain it.

description:
People will confidently explain a choice they never made.
In a 2005 study published in Science, Petter Johansson, Lars Hall and colleagues at Lund University in Sweden showed 120 volunteers pairs of photographs of faces and asked them to pick the more attractive one. On some trials the experimenter used a double-card magic trick to hand back the face the volunteer had not chosen. Only about one swap in eight was caught immediately, and roughly three quarters were never detected. Asked why they had chosen 'their' photo, volunteers gave reasons with the same confidence, detail and emotion as for genuine choices. The team called the effect choice blindness, and later found it in taste tests of jam and tea, where fewer than a third of swaps were detected.
Do you think you would have noticed? Comment below.
first_comment: The same team later swapped jam and tea in a supermarket tasting. Fewer than a third of the swaps were caught. Would you have noticed?
